layers.title: Old inns
layers.intro: Three pubs in the centre each claim to be the oldest in Nottingham. A television investigation concluded that the Salutation is the oldest building, but the Bell has been a pub the longest.

layers.title: Churches
layers.intro: Medieval Nottingham had three parishes: St Mary's, St Peter's and St Nicholas'. Each still has its church, joined in the 1840s by a Catholic cathedral, and by chapels of the Nonconformists, such as the Unitarians on High Pavement.

layers.title: Lace and trade
layers.intro: In the 19th century Nottingham was a world centre of lace. Merchants built warehouses and showrooms in the Lace Market, east of the Old Market Square.

layers.title: Civic Nottingham
layers.intro: The buildings where the town and county were governed, judged and connected to the railway.

layers.title: Theatres and culture
layers.intro: Theatres, concert halls, a library and galleries, from a Georgian subscription library to a 21st-century art centre.

layers.title: Wilford
layers.intro: A village on the south bank of the Trent, reached for centuries by ferry and, since the 1870s, by bridge.

layers.title: West Bridgford and Trent Bridge
layers.intro: South of the river: Test cricket, Nottingham Forest and the county's headquarters.

layers.title: The Meadows and the river
layers.intro: The low ground between the city and the Trent, with two football grounds facing each other across the river.

layers.title: Clifton
layers.intro: An old village above the Trent, and next to it one of the largest housing estates ever built by a council.

layers.title: Sneinton
layers.intro: The hill east of the city: a windmill, cave dwellings, a church by Thomas Rickman and the old wholesale market.

layers.title: Caves
layers.intro: Nottingham stands on soft sandstone that can be dug with hand tools, and about a thousand man-made caves are known beneath it: cellars, workshops, dwellings and shelters.

layers.title: People
layers.intro: People connected with buildings on the map: who designed them, who lived, worked or played in them, and who is remembered on their walls. Entries come from commemorative plaques (Open Plaques), architects recorded in Wikidata, and hand-written entries checked against Wikipedia and Historic England.

layers.title: Barton in Fabis and Thrumpton
layers.intro: Two villages on the south bank of the Trent, upstream from Clifton: Barton, once Barton in the Beans, and Thrumpton, with its Jacobean hall.

layers.title: Rushcliffe
layers.intro: The borough south of the Trent: villages of stocking knitters, a Tudor hall and the gravel pits that became a centre for watersports, a Civil War massacre and the regicide who led it, the village of fools, an airfield, a mining village, and the last coal-fired power station in Britain.

layers.title: Science and industry
layers.intro: Where Nottingham invented, made and mined: from the stocking frame to the bicycle, the medicines of Boots, the scanner that sees inside the body, and the water, coal and shells the city depended on.

layers.title: The industrial revolution
layers.intro: How Nottingham and its coalfield helped make the industrial age: an early railway of wood, the first mill of the factory system, the canal and the railway that carried the coal, the lace machine, the frame-breakers who fought the machines, and the iron and steam that outlasted the pits.

properties.name: Bendigo's tomb
properties.text: William "Bendigo" Thompson, born in Nottingham on 11 October 1811, won the heavyweight championship of England in 1839. He died in 1880 and was buried in St Mary's burial ground, under a tomb with a crouching lion. The city of Bendigo in Australia is indirectly named after him.

properties.name: Curzon Street
properties.text: Mary Kendrick, the tidal engineer who led the studies of river levels and silt for the Thames Barrier, grew up on Curzon Street, where her father was a haulage contractor. She later kept the Mersey navigable as its Acting Conservator.

properties.name: The suffragettes' office, Carlton Street
properties.text: Nellie Crocker was the suffragettes' organiser in Nottingham from 1909 to 1912, with an office on Carlton Street. After her eighth arrest, for attacking a post office in London, she spent three months of 1912 in Holloway.

properties.name: 21 Regent Street
properties.text: Sarah Gray, Nottingham's first woman GP, lived and practised at 21 Regent Street. At the Women's Hospital from 1899 she was refused charge of in-patients; in 1921 she became the first president of the Nottingham Medico-Chirurgical Society.

properties.name: 15 Regent Street
properties.text: Margaret Glen-Bott (1891–1969) came to Nottingham in 1916. The first woman gynaecologist to be Honorary Surgeon at the Women's Hospital and the Children's Hospital, and later a magistrate, she lived at 15 Regent Street.

properties.name: The Girls' Friendly Society hostel, 4–6 Regent Street
properties.text: From 1913, at the Girls' Friendly Society hostel at 4–6 Regent Street, Constance Penswick Smith (1878–1938) worked to revive Mothering Sunday, with the hostel's superintendent, Ellen Porter.

properties.name: 18 High Pavement
properties.text: Ruth Bryan (1805–1860) came to Nottingham as a child with her father, a minister. She lived at 18 High Pavement and kept a detailed diary from 1822.

properties.name: Old Market Square
properties.text: One of the largest paved squares in the United Kingdom. The two towns were once divided by a wall across it, whose line a stainless steel channel now marks; Goose Fair was held here until 1928.

properties.name: Broad Marsh
properties.text: After large-scale slum clearance, the Broad Marsh shopping centre was officially opened on 25 March 1975. It closed in 2020 and was left partially demolished; caves found beneath it, dug into the soft sandstone, became part of the City of Caves.

properties.name: Wilford Power Station
properties.text: A coal-fired power station on the north bank of the Trent, opened in 1925. It closed in 1981 and was soon demolished; the Riverside Retail Park stands on its site.

properties.name: The Nottingham Captain
properties.text: Jeremiah Brandreth, born in Wilford, led the Pentrich rising of 1817 and was known as the Nottingham Captain. He was hanged for high treason outside Derby Gaol that November, and then beheaded.

properties.name: Captain John Deane
properties.text: Captain John Deane, a former mercenary who had served in the Russian navy, retired to Wilford.

properties.name: Trent Bridge cricket ground
properties.text: The first recorded match was played on ground behind the Trent Bridge Inn in 1838, and William Clarke opened the ground in 1841. It hosted its first Test match, England against Australia, in 1899.

properties.name: City Ground
properties.text: Nottingham Forest moved here in 1898, to their seventh home. The name dates from 1897, when Nottingham was granted city status, and Notts County's Meadow Lane is only three hundred yards away, on the other side of the Trent.

properties.name: A fort at the bridge
properties.text: The settlement began in the early 10th century, when defences and houses were built at the south end of Trent Bridge to guard Nottingham against the Danes. Domesday, in 1086, records it as part of the manor of Clifton.

properties.name: Won at cards
properties.text: The Musters family gained the West Bridgford estate in 1523, reputedly by winning it in a game of cards. When they sold land for building they set strict rules for it, and the village grew into a suburb, with its own council from 1894 and part of the borough of Rushcliffe from 1972.

properties.name: Edwalton station
properties.text: The station opened in 1880 on the Midland Railway's direct line from Nottingham to Melton Mowbray, which let its London expresses avoid Leicester. It closed to passengers in 1941, and its site is now housing. Beyond it the line became the Old Dalby test track, where the Advanced Passenger Train was tried.

properties.name: Compton Acres
properties.text: A district built mostly in the 1990s, named after a garden in Poole. Its tram, opened in 2015, runs along a disused railway line.

properties.name: The first Test, 1899
properties.text: The first Test at Trent Bridge, England against Australia in June 1899, was W. G. Grace's last Test and Wilfred Rhodes's first.

source.title: Australian cricket team in England in 1899

properties.name: The Lady Bay bombs
properties.text: In 1941 a German bomber dropped a line of bombs across Lady Bay. New houses went up on the bomb sites in the 1950s and 1960s, and Pinders Ponds, to the east, are thought to be flooded bomb craters.

properties.name: Meadow Lane
properties.text: Notts County moved here on 3 September 1910. Divided by the Trent, Meadow Lane and the City Ground are the closest pair of football grounds in England.

properties.name: Victoria Embankment
properties.text: A mile and a quarter of flood defences along the Trent, built between 1898 and 1901 under the borough engineer Arthur Brown. Part of it was later laid out as Memorial Gardens to the dead of the First World War.

properties.name: The Meadows rebuilt
properties.text: Much of the Meadows' pre-1919 terraced housing was demolished to make way for a new development of modern council housing, and the viaduct carrying the Great Central railway came down in 1975.

properties.name: Clifton estate
properties.text: Planned from 1950, the Clifton council estate was at one time the largest council estate in Europe. Since the 1980s most of its houses have passed into private ownership.

properties.name: Clifton Grove
properties.text: The Nottingham poet Henry Kirke White, a butcher's son, published Clifton Grove, a Sketch in Verse, in 1803, aged 17. He died in 1806, aged 21.

properties.name: Sneinton Market
properties.text: In the 1930s the city's wholesale fruit and vegetable market moved here from the Old Market Square.

properties.name: Mortimer's Hole
properties.text: A long passage to the bottom of the castle rock is known as Mortimer's Hole. In October 1330 Edward III's men came in by a secret tunnel, and Roger Mortimer was led out bound and gagged.

properties.name: Sneinton Hermitage
properties.text: Cave dwellings dug into the sandstone ridge extended out into Sneinton, where they were known as the Hermitage. What little remains can still be seen along Sneinton Hermitage.

properties.name: Barton in the Beans
properties.text: The village's older name was Barton in the Beans, after the beans grown here; fabis is Latin for beans. A ferry crossed the Trent from here to Attenborough from before 1774. Today Fairham, a new district, is being built in the parish beside Clifton.

properties.name: An estate village
properties.text: Many of Thrumpton's gabled brick houses were built for the estate by John Emerton of Thrumpton Hall, up to 1745.

properties.name: National Watersports Centre
properties.text: Dug out of a former gravel works, the centre opened in 1971, and hosted the World Rowing Championships in 1975 and 1986. Its whitewater course was built in 1986.

properties.name: The lost church of Flawford
properties.text: St Peter's, the old church of Flawford, closed in 1718 and was pulled down in 1779. Three alabaster figures found in it, probably hidden around 1539, are now at Nottingham Castle Museum, and Ruddington's chapel took its name.

properties.name: The storming of Shelford House
properties.text: In November 1645 Parliament's troops under Sydnam Poyntz, with Colonel John Hutchinson leading the assault, stormed Shelford House, held for the King by Philip Stanhope. About 160 of its defenders were killed, and the house was burnt that night.

properties.name: Colonel Hutchinson
properties.text: John Hutchinson, born at Owthorpe in 1615, held Nottingham Castle for Parliament from 1643 and signed Charles I's death warrant. He died a prisoner in 1664 and is buried at Owthorpe; his wife Lucy's Memoirs of his life made him famous.

properties.name: The Wise Men of Gotham
properties.text: A legend says that the villagers played the fool, even trying to fence in a cuckoo, so that King John would build his road and hunting lodge elsewhere. In 1807 Washington Irving called New York "Gotham", and Batman's Gotham City took the name.

properties.name: Cotgrave Colliery
properties.text: The colliery came in the early 1960s: from 1962 hundreds of mining families moved here from Radford's closed pit, and the village grew several times over. The pit worked through the 1984–85 strike and closed in 1993.

properties.name: Ratcliffe-on-Soar Power Station
properties.text: Generating from 1968, with eight cooling towers, it was the last coal-fired power station in Britain. When it shut in September 2024 it ended 142 years of coal power in the country.

properties.name: The stocking frame
properties.text: In 1589 William Lee of Calverton invented the stocking frame, a machine that knitted. Legend has it that Elizabeth I refused him a patent. The trade grew here, and from 1728 Nottingham was one of its main centres.

properties.name: Raleigh Street
properties.text: In 1885 a small bicycle workshop opened in Raleigh Street, and it gave the company its name. Frank Bowden took it over in 1888, and by 1897 Raleigh had a purpose-built works of seven and a half acres on Faraday Road.

properties.name: Papplewick Pumping Station
properties.text: Built in 1881–1884 to pump drinking water for Nottingham from deep wells, with two beam engines by James Watt & Co. and an engine house by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton, ornate with cast iron and stained glass. It pumped until 1969 and opened as a museum in 1976.

properties.name: National Shell Filling Factory
properties.text: Viscount Chetwynd built the factory from 1915 to fill shells with explosive; it filled some 19 million during the First World War. On 1 July 1918 eight tons of TNT exploded, killing 134 people. The site is now Chetwynd Barracks.

properties.name: Gedling Colliery
properties.text: Gedling Colliery closed in 1991, and in 2015 its grounds became Gedling Country Park.

properties.name: Wollaton Wagonway
properties.text: In 1603–1604 Huntingdon Beaumont and Sir Percival Willoughby laid a wooden wagonway from the Strelley coal pits to Wollaton Lane End, its wagons drawn by horses. It is described as the first railway in Britain.

properties.name: Arkwright's first mill
properties.text: Richard Arkwright's first cotton mill opened in Nottingham in 1768, its machines turned by horses. By 1772 it had four storeys and 300 workers.

properties.name: The first Luddites
properties.text: The Luddite movement began in Arnold on 11 March 1811. Across Nottinghamshire the frame-breakers went after the "wide" knitting frames used to make cheap goods.

properties.name: Lowe's Silk Mill
properties.text: During the Reform riots of 1831, Lowe's Silk Mill in Beeston was burnt on 11 October, the day after Nottingham Castle, and the same day the riots ceased.

properties.name: Great Central Railway (Nottingham)
properties.text: Great Central Railway (Nottingham) opened between 1990 and 1999. Subject: transport: trains and railways.
